disclosure.title: Confidentiality & Disclosure Note
disclosure.text: I conducted the following four projects through Duke University collaborations from September 2023 to September 2026. Partner names and proprietary internal system identifiers are withheld under nondisclosure agreements. The collaborators include a leading multimodal foundation model developer, a frontier AI research laboratory, and a leading global alternative asset manager with more than $300 billion in assets under management. The project titles, my role as a researcher, locations, dates, system architectures, mathematical formulations, and reproducible synthetic benchmarks are cleared for public disclosure.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Foundation Model Developer
entries.summary: Beginning in September 2023, I led the development of a large-scale domain expert collaboration system for LLM post-training, defining reusable mathematical specifications and operating standards for expert feedback production. The system coordinated more than 300 specialists across several domains and an external vendor network supporting reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) *(the corporate partner is anonymized under NDA; my role, project scope, and mathematical design are approved for public disclosure)*. I brought contributor reliability calibration, evolving acceptance criteria, and review capacity allocation into a common framework. It combines hierarchical Beta-Binomial modeling, prediction-assisted active statistical inference with inverse-probability-weighted residual correction, and capacity-constrained mixed-integer programming to optimize the *statistical value of measuring population quality* and the *value of correcting defects* separately. In a synthetic benchmark of 10,000 submissions evaluated over 200,000 independent sampling repetitions, the allocation method reduced population quality estimation variance by **17.79%** relative to uniform sampling at the same expected audit cost, under ideal residual calibration. A separate analytical example with 200 tasks reduced expected post-review error loss by **8.89%** at the same review volume.
entries.detailTitle: Large-scale domain expert feedback governance and adaptive review

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **Beginning in September 2023, I led the development of a collaboration system spanning more than 300 domain experts across several specialties.** I defined the mathematical specifications and operating standards for task organization, reliability calibration, acceptance adjudication, and review allocation across the project's external expert and vendor networks. These procedures made distributed expert judgments traceable and subject to calibration as post-training feedback.

**I designed tiered review rules using Beta-Binomial reliability posteriors, credible intervals, verified sample counts, and task-level risk priors.** In one workflow, flagged submissions were dynamically assigned to three additional specialists, while initially accepted submissions went to one or two. Expert adjudications then updated contributor reliability posteriors, informed targeted coaching, and adjusted review intensity.

**I combined independent random reference audits with escalation of high-risk tasks to turn recurring annotator disagreements into explicit acceptance criteria.** I distinguished missing context, ambiguous instructions, and contributor errors, then revised task instructions, boundary cases, and shared calibration anchors. Subsequent comparisons of Dawid-Skene reviewer-error models and cost-sensitive deferral rules (DeCCaF) informed escalation thresholds.

**I built SQL and Python pipelines that brought together task metadata, review histories, acceptance outcomes, turnaround times, and behavioral logs, and reconciled platform activity with Hubstaff operational telemetry.** These records supplied empirical estimates of unit verification costs ($c_i$), task-stratum latencies ($t_{iaj}$), and hard specialist capacity limits ($H_j^{\text{review}}$) for the allocation solvers. I also translated client-reported model defects into reproducible engineering investigations and standard operating procedures.

**I formalized the production procedures by connecting prediction-assisted active statistical inference, cost-aware audit allocation, and capacity-constrained review assignment.** The analysis defines a task's *initial error risk* ($q_i$), the *statistical information value of an independent reference audit* ($m_i / c_i$), and the *expected defect loss removable through additional human handling* ($\Delta_i = r_{i0} - r_{i1}$). I derived the sampling and review decisions associated with each quantity, producing a reusable allocation method for expert feedback across domains.

**I tested the estimator and allocation algorithms on a stratified synthetic benchmark of 10,000 submissions using 200,000 independent Monte Carlo sampling repetitions.** Under ideal residual calibration and an equal expected audit budget, allocation based on residuals and costs reduced population quality estimation variance by **17.79%**, equivalent to a **9.33%** reduction in standard deviation, relative to uniform sampling. In a separate analytical example with 200 tasks, ranking reviews by marginal gain reduced expected post-review defect loss by **8.89%** at the same review volume.

architecturalContext.title: Architectural Context: Statistical governance for expert data production
architecturalContext.text: Beginning in September 2023, I led the development of the project's expert feedback governance framework for post-training across multiple domains. I coordinated hundreds of distributed specialists and external vendor queues and defined mathematical specifications for quality measurement and resource allocation under selective review. When review successfully targets tasks with higher true error probabilities, the resulting selection bias is positive ($\operatorname{Cov}(\pi(X), q(X)) > 0$), so raw inspection error rates require correction before they can support population quality inference. Audit allocation must also account for residual uncertainty and verification cost to direct expert capacity toward tasks that improve estimation precision. The following seven sections formalize the production design and compare it with subsequent literature. September 2023 is the collaboration's start date; references published in 2024 to 2026 provide later methodological context.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Foundation Model Developer
entries.summary: This project began in September 2023 as part of a frontier foundation model program *(the partner's identity is confidential under an NDA)*. I defined the requirements for high-signal financial post-training data and developed a framework covering adversarial task design, constraint-preserving synthetic data, and structured preference supervision. To identify subtle reasoning errors that recur in both foundation models and professional practice, I designed diagnostic financial decision tasks and a five-level pairwise preference protocol. The protocol translates judgments from experts with doctoral or CFA-level expertise into evidence-based training signals for reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and direct preference optimization. I paired these task specifications with mathematical synthesis methods for four settings: Gaussian copulas for cross-sectional corporate fundamentals; covariance-weighted affine projections for exact accounting identities, with a maximum residual of $1.21 \times 10^{-14}$ across 200,000 12-dimensional draws; CTGAN and TabDDPM for multimodal tables, with Lipschitz decision-margin checks and Gaussian margin-to-noise analysis ($\gamma/s$) to guide label recomputation; and stochastic differential equations (SDEs), neural SDEs, and Brownian bridges for continuous-time price and interest-rate paths, with strict separation of temporal information sets ($\mathcal{F}_s$). I created **Batch Zero** to translate the capability objectives and data requirements of post-training research teams into a data strategy with explicit criteria for independent execution and expert calibration before scaling. The protocol tests whether task specifications, reference solutions, and preference annotations can be reproduced, then uses execution disagreements to refine task design and data acceptance criteria. The company subsequently extended Batch Zero to other new post-training programs.
entries.detailTitle: Financial task design and synthetic data engineering

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **Beginning in September 2023, I led financial and business decision task design for a frontier foundation model program, specifying the capability taxonomy, primary evidence standards, input schemas, decisive variables, and acceptance criteria.** Diagnostic cases targeted high-stakes business decision boundaries where foundation models and practitioners repeatedly make errors. The cases translated doctoral or CFA-level domain judgment into testable task requirements.

**I designed a five-level pairwise preference protocol for RLHF and DPO supervision.** The protocol records why an expert prefers one response to another and turns domain knowledge into post-training supervision. Each judgment must cite verifiable evidence, relevant accounting rules, and decisive variables. These annotations preserve the evidence and reasoning behind each preference and support training models to assess whether a financial judgment has sufficient support.
**I developed financial synthetic data methods for four settings.** I selected and adapted mathematical generators to each task's structural invariants, data types, and permitted information:

**I created Batch Zero to implement post-training data strategy.** Starting from the capability objectives and data requirements of post-training research teams, I established a protocol for independent execution and expert calibration before a task family enters large-scale data construction. Doctoral-level domain experts independently construct tasks, generate synthetic variants, solve reference cases, and assign five-level pairwise preference scores. Execution disagreements and failure modes inform revisions to task specifications, boundary cases, and **Batch One** data acceptance criteria. The foundation model company subsequently extended **Batch Zero** to other new post-training programs.

**I quantified stale-label errors, temporal leakage, and task-family clustering.** Analytical derivations and simulations show that synthetic perturbations near a decision boundary produce **40.13%** inherited-label error at $\gamma/s = 0.25$ when labels are not recomputed. Undisclosed Brownian bridge endpoint conditioning creates an apparent **29.29% reduction in RMSE** through future-information leakage. With within-family correlation $\rho = 0.5$, 2,000 nominal synthetic variants from 100 task families provide only **$N_{\text{eff}} \approx 190.48$** effective independent observations.

architecturalContext.title: Architectural Context: Task specifications and data strategy for financial post-training
architecturalContext.text:
In September 2023, frontier foundation models could reproduce corporate finance definitions but still made unpredictable errors in financial workflows where a small numerical change or an accounting footnote could reverse an investment recommendation. I developed a data strategy around the capability objectives and data requirements of post-training research teams, connecting task specifications, synthesis methods, and expert calibration to address two problems:
1. **Diagnosing reasoning limits through task design.** Simple prompts may provide little basis for distinguishing candidate responses. We designed prompts around subtle business failure modes, including covenant breaches, off-balance-sheet adjustments, and valuation differences close to a decision boundary. Paired with the five-level preference protocol, these prompts turn domain judgments such as *"Response A is better because it isolates the working-capital constraint and cites Footnote 4"* into structured preference supervision for post-training.
2. **Matching the generator to the financial structure.** Synthetic financial data must satisfy structural constraints, remain consistent with reference judgments, and respect the task's information boundaries. A corporate table that violates Total Assets $=$ Total Liabilities $+$ Equity, even by a fraction of a percentage point, introduces a structural error. An interest-rate path that exposes a future terminal rate to a historical forecasting task introduces temporal leakage. Sections 1 through 6 state the conditions, analytical results, and validation designs for each method. Batch Zero turns these requirements into acceptance criteria: experts must be able to execute the task specification independently, reproduce reference solutions, and calibrate their judgments.

items: *Cross-sectional corporate fundamentals.* I used Gaussian and vine copulas with conditional sampling for company size, operating history, and financial ratios. These methods preserve joint dependencies across columns and avoid the unrealistic combinations produced by sampling each column independently.

*Accounting identities, ratio bounds, and chronological order.* Constrained sampling, variable transformations, and covariance-weighted affine projections enforce balance-sheet and cash-flow identities, ratio ranges, and date ordering. Across 200,000 12-dimensional synthetic draws, the maximum constraint residual was **$1.21 \times 10^{-14}$**. A separate standardized-residual rejection model had an acceptance rate of $0.0002529\%$.

*Multimodal records with numerical and categorical fields.* CTGAN and TabDDPM model multimodal empirical distributions. Mandatory business-rule checks after generation, Lipschitz decision-margin tests, and Gaussian margin-to-noise analysis ($\gamma/s$) guide reference-answer recomputation and reduce stale supervision labels.

*Continuous-time price and interest-rate paths.* SDEs, neural SDEs, Brownian bridges, and stochastic interpolation generate paths for temporal financial tasks; static cross-sectional company comparisons do not require these constructions. This work extends MathWorks-style stochastic interest-rate path construction and matches each method to the task's permitted filtration ($\mathcal{F}_s$) to prevent future-information leakage in evaluation.

entries.organization: Duke University × Frontier AI Research Laboratory
entries.summary: I developed a framework for evaluating and supervising general reasoning through a university collaboration with a frontier AI research laboratory that began in September 2023 (partner identity withheld under NDA). The evaluation brings together task specifications, the model's visible chain of thought (CoT), and evidence from execution. I examine final answers alongside reasoning traces, tool calls, intermediate outputs, elapsed time, and attempt counts to identify unsupported claims, misapplied rules, and repeated attempts that make no progress. The review process has three layers: code or rules check directly verifiable answers and hard requirements; LLM-as-a-Judge screens for semantic issues; and scholars with relevant expertise review domain judgments and disputed cases. Proof-obligation dependency graphs, checkable mathematical certificates, and error-propagation rules for task transformations make the resulting supervision signals traceable. Correctness, compliance with execution requirements, and efficiency are recorded separately. I also used exact-arithmetic stress tests to examine whether certificate rules detect errors while accepting valid alternative proofs, and analyzed how grading bias propagates into post-training objectives.
entries.detailTitle: General reasoning evaluation and layered verification

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **I developed a joint evaluation method for answers, visible reasoning, and execution evidence.** Beginning in September 2023, I brought the model's displayed CoT, actual tool calls, and intermediate outputs into the review workflow, assessing the validity of conclusions, compliance with task requirements, and progress during problem solving as separate dimensions.

**I organized deliverables into proof-obligation dependency graphs ($\Gamma_q \vdash C_q$).** The graphs track domain assumptions, method applicability, evidentiary support, compliant execution, uniform approximation bounds, and the strength of each conclusion. They help locate the first unsupported step and its downstream effects while allowing valid alternative derivations. For tasks that admit formalization, checking local nodes and their dependencies within a sound inference system establishes the full conclusion.

**I developed checkable error certificates and bounds on solution quality for programmatically verifiable task families under explicit mathematical assumptions.** The projected-residual optimality bound ($0 \le f(x) - v^* \le \|P_{\ker A} r\|_2^2 / (2\mu)$) makes feasibility, stationarity, and the accuracy of a conclusion separate verification obligations. Different proofs can pass by satisfying the same obligations. Section 3 gives the assumptions, certificate construction, and problem class.

**I established a division of work among code or rule checks, LLM-assisted screening, and review by scholars with relevant expertise.** Code checks directly verifiable answers, tool permissions, and other requirements specified in advance. LLM-as-a-Judge helps flag missing evidence, misapplied rules, and gaps in reasoning; disputed domain judgments go to specialist scholars. I also compare elapsed time, attempt counts, changes in intermediate outputs, and the use of tool results to identify redundant work and loops without progress. These efficiency findings remain separate from correctness judgments.

**I derived how false acceptance ($\alpha$) and false rejection ($\beta$) can reverse model rankings and bias the binary cross-entropy gradient used to train process reward models ($E[\nabla_s \ell(s,V) - \nabla_s \ell(s,Z) \mid h] = p(h) - \tilde{p}(h)$).** I also derived the exact tolerance-propagation rule ($a\delta + 2\varepsilon$) for bijective task transformations. These results specify when grading labels and transformed tasks support valid comparisons.

**I tested false acceptance and false rejection on 3,600 exact-arithmetic submissions from 600 constructed strongly convex quadratic task families.** In this benchmark, 75% of invalid proofs reported the correct final value. Certificate checking accepted all 1,200 valid proofs (0.0% false rejection) and rejected all 2,400 invalid submissions (0.0% false acceptance). Final-answer matching had a 75.0% false acceptance rate, while strict reference-path matching had a 50.0% false rejection rate. The constructed families defined in Section 6 test both error detection and the retention of valid alternative proofs.

architecturalContext.title: Architectural Context: Visible reasoning and execution evidence
architecturalContext.text: The collaboration began in fall 2023 with an evaluation of general reasoning in frontier models. In our workflow, a correct answer could coexist with unsupported assumptions, misapplied rules, or tool use that violated the task specification. Repeated calls that left the evidence and intermediate results unchanged also exposed opportunities to improve execution. I therefore cross-checked final answers, the model's visible reasoning, execution records, and efficiency measures, with responsibilities divided among programmatic checks, LLM-assisted semantic screening, and review by specialist scholars. Sections 1 through 7 describe the acceptance criteria, mathematical certificates for a programmatically verifiable subfamily, and the associated experiments. The collaboration's start date does not imply that every later citation or mathematical formulation was part of the initial workflow.

items: I cross-check the model's displayed CoT against actual tool calls, return values, and intermediate outputs to assess whether its reasoning claims have observable support.
I use code or rules to check directly verifiable answers, required deliverables, and approved tools and execution environments. Compliance is assessed against the requirements specified for the task.

I use elapsed time, attempt counts, and changes in intermediate results to identify repeated operations, continued use of failed assumptions, and attempts that add no evidence. These findings inform efficiency analysis even when the final answer is correct. Any resource limit used to determine acceptance must be defined in the task specification beforehand.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Global Alternative Asset Manager
entries.summary: I developed and implemented an evidence verification and decision assurance framework through a multiyear collaboration between Duke University and a leading global alternative asset manager with more than $300 billion in assets under management. The partner is unnamed under a confidentiality agreement. The research examines how AI-polished disclosures and corporate narratives affect ESG and investment scores, accounting jointly for model selection, unverified claims, and shared reporting errors. The system ingests evidence from multiple sources, scores companies across a Rashomon model set, and computes support-function bounds on ranking stability. A minimax-regret criterion directs analysts to the facts they should verify next; versioned updates then propagate corrections through scores and SHAP attributions. In reproducible analytical benchmarks, the joint model certified a 0.6-point pairwise company advantage that separate company intervals could not establish. In an eight-scenario benchmark with one equal-cost query, the verification criterion reduced worst-case decision regret from 0.61 score units to zero.
entries.detailTitle: Evidence verification and robust comparison in investment research
keyContributions: **I studied how AI-polished corporate narratives influence LLM-assisted scoring, ESG ratings, and investment analysis when the underlying claims lack factual support.** I brought corporate claims, cross-document contradictions, and shared reporting errors into a common review process to support targeted verification in private-market and ESG research.

**I translated institutional diligence requirements into measures of score reliability, pairwise ranking stability, and verification priority.** I implemented a workflow that ingests evidence, scores companies across a Rashomon model set, computes ranking bounds, and allocates verification effort using minimax regret. Corrections trigger rescoring and attribution updates, giving the investment committee a traceable basis for its analysis.

**I converted operating reports, audited financial statements, sustainability disclosures, management questionnaires, and third-party datasets into structured scoring rules with source and version records.** AI-assisted checks identify unsupported claims and contradictions across documents for targeted factual review.

**I deployed gradient-boosted trees and deep learning models for tabular data to capture nonlinear thresholds and interactions.** SHAP attributions across a near-optimal Rashomon set ($\mathcal{F}_\alpha$), together with conditional Shapley analysis, measure sensitivity to model choice and identify scoring factors whose contributions remain stable across models.

**I derived failure cases for conventional bootstrap resampling and verification priorities based on raw SHAP magnitudes when inputs contain shared reporting bias or unverified claims.** I represented unresolved evidence $\mathcal{X}(E)$ jointly with the Rashomon set $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ through $\Omega(E) = \mathcal{F}_\alpha \times \mathcal{X}(E)$ and derived convex support-function bounds ($h_U(a_f)$). Common measurement errors cancel when the two companies have identical exposures. In a synthetic comparison, the joint model certified a 0.6-point advantage that the difference bound from separate company intervals ($[-1.4, 2.6]$) could not establish.

**I derived a query criterion that requires no probability distribution over scenarios within the specified joint uncertainty set.** It prioritizes the reduction in worst-case decision regret that a query can guarantee. For unequal query costs, $V(q)/c_q$ provides a one-step efficiency measure. In an eight-scenario benchmark with one equal-cost query, targeted verification reduced worst-case regret from 0.61 score units to zero; rechecking an already verified feature with a large SHAP attribution reduced regret by zero.

architecturalContext.title: Architectural Context: Corporate evidence and the allocation of verification effort
architecturalContext.text: Institutional diligence must account for uncertainty in both corporate evidence and scoring models. AI-polished narratives, unverified sustainability claims, and common reporting errors can all affect ESG and investment scores. The architecture takes a traceable evidence state as its input and incorporates model multiplicity, joint measurement error, and verification costs. Sections 1 through 6 set out the limits of attribution methods, the joint uncertainty model, ranking bounds, the query criterion, versioned updates, and analytical benchmarks.

entries.summary: Owned business development for Jiritsu's asset-verification and privacy-preserving computation services as the sole dedicated contributor for new issuers. Reported directly to a co-founder, combining data engineering, preference ranking, and counterparty discussions to develop partnership recommendations for the board.
keyContributions: Served as the sole dedicated contributor to business development for new issuers, reporting to co-founder Asher Gottesman. Turned commercialization priorities into screening criteria, experiments, data requirements, and outreach plans; independently managed analysis, counterparty discussions, and recommendations.

Organized core-team reviews with commercial input from Asher Gottesman and technical and financial guidance from Gene Itkis of MIT Lincoln Laboratory and Michael Lustig, former Senior Managing Director at BlackRock and Adjunct Professor of Finance at NYU Stern. Assessed applied cryptography, zero-knowledge applications, technical fit, liquidity, and risk.

Designed a two-stage framework for real-world assets, stablecoins, DeFi, and infrastructure: test identity, liquidity, pricing validity, data completeness, and risk, then rank commercial fit and accessibility. Used issuer-level error analysis to refine qualification rules, exclude out-of-scope projects, and record evidence-backed reasons for each decision.

Resolved issuer identities across CoinGecko, chain records, websites, white papers, and disclosures. Reconciled multichain listings and wrapped or bridged assets to remove duplicate opportunities. Built market and text features spanning liquidity, capitalization, activity, project age, chain affiliation, business models, and technical needs.

Built a Python, Prefect, DuckDB, and Parquet pipeline for ingestion, standardization, entity mapping, feature preparation, and querying. Implemented scheduled refreshes, retries, persisted outputs, reruns, and historical backfills to support model training and repeatable shortlist updates.

Trained a LightGBM pairwise ranking model on the core team's comparisons of eligible counterparties. Combined commercial, disclosure, and market features to prioritize approximately 800 potential partners. Repeated comparison, retraining, and ranking over two to four weeks, using uncertainty sampling to focus expert review on borderline candidates, near ties, and conflicting evidence.

Applied issuer similarity analysis and Leiden community detection to discover overlooked projects with related business or technical characteristics, then brought qualified candidates into commercial review and ranking.

Led Codex-assisted solution design and Python development. Used meta prompting and ChatGPT deep research to translate business objectives into analytical plans and development specifications; selected methods, debugged workflows, and verified issuer-level outputs and selection rationales.

Screened 18,000+ token records into approximately 800 potential counterparties, 30 outreach priorities, and six proposed pilot counterparties. Discussed asset-verification needs, service arrangements, and technology licensing with prospects, and delivered the candidate list and commercial assessments to the board for technical and business evaluation.

entries.summary: Led the China workstream of a global market-entry engagement covering China, Japan, and the Middle East for a premium European appliance brand. Combined market data, consumer evidence, and policy research to recommend local products, pricing, channels, and marketing while maintaining the client's global positioning.
entries.detailTitle: China Market Entry for a Premium European Appliance Brand
keyContributions: Built a MECE analytical framework spanning product fit, pricing, channels, marketing, and policy. Defined which elements of the client's premium positioning should remain consistent globally and where the China strategy required local adaptation.

Specified data requirements across five e-commerce platforms and seven appliance categories, coordinating with data scientists on collection and local analysts on validation. Owned downstream processing and interpretation of approximately 50,000 listings in Python, standardizing attributes, efficiency labels, prices, promotions, and reviews while preserving channel-specific observations.

Mapped competitors in Tableau by category, price band, efficiency, and features. Combined product comparisons with consumer reviews to identify relatively underserved segments, including high-efficiency products at mid- to high-price points, and assessed opportunities in tier-1 and tier-2 cities.

Evaluated the European portfolio against Chinese usage needs, product dimensions, and efficiency requirements. Recommended local assortments and compared the brand's website, e-commerce, physical retail, and channel partnerships, incorporating Xiaohongshu and Douyin into marketing analysis.

Researched efficiency standards, subsidies, certification, and market access through published sources and expert interviews, including think-tank discussions. Built entry scenarios by category and city tier, translating current requirements and expected policy changes into product-introduction and timing recommendations.

Delivered the China market report and represented the workstream in global project meetings. Presented the evidence behind product, pricing, channel, and marketing recommendations; coordinated green-product definitions and policy assumptions. Documented field mappings and processing rules in a reusable template for subsequent regional analysis.
Received a full-time offer from Euromonitor's consulting team during the internship.

entries.summary: Applied statistical methods to sustainability assessment and green-credit screening within China Construction Bank's internal framework. Combined company data, historical assessments, and explicit eligibility rules to support candidate review, then documented the method for product managers and risk officers evaluating its use on a platform.
entries.detailTitle: PCA-Based Sustainability Analysis and Green-Credit Screening
keyContributions: Analyzed financial, operational, and environmental data for approximately 2,000 entities within CCB's framework of more than 30 indicators, assessing overall scores alongside minimum requirements for individual metrics.

Used PCA to identify overlapping indicator information and construct compact representations for candidate comparison. Applied supervised learning to historically labeled cases, examining feature patterns associated with positive and negative assessments and adding empirical evidence to candidate assessment.
Incorporated life cycle assessment principles into sustainability analysis, examining operating and environmental factors alongside financial performance.
Tested the initial top 30% of ranked candidates against individual-metric and overall-score minimums, retaining approximately 28% of the full pool for further research and review.

Reviewed selection and exclusion patterns across the pool, separating ranking cutoffs from threshold failures. Converted borderline cases, unmet requirements, and follow-up questions into a reusable checklist linked to the applicable screening rules.
Delivered a methodology note explaining scoring logic, data sources, model behavior, and edge cases to product managers and risk officers assessing the method for platform use.

entries.organization: Autonomous Authority in Space: Risk Tradeoffs and the Law of Delegation
entries.summary: Developed a legal framework for authorizing autonomous space operations when delayed human intervention creates risks of its own. Formulated a two-threshold test separating the authority to act from the evidence needed to delegate execution. Applied it to delayed spacecraft operations, orbital avoidance, debris capture, and SETI, then proposed task-specific authorization records. The resulting framework identifies which decisions can be authorized in advance, which require renewed review, and what evidence must support each choice.
entries.detailTitle: Autonomous Authority in Space: Risk Tradeoffs and the Law of Delegation
keyContributions: Specified a decision procedure linking legal authority, evidence for delegation, and the time at which human review can still change the outcome. Distinguished individual approval, advance-constrained action, and fallback behavior as separate supervisory choices.

Designed an authorization record specifying responsible actors, permitted actions, operating conditions, exposed interests, and reassessment triggers. Connected these terms to independent scrutiny and event records that allow consequential decisions to be reconstructed.

Compared delayed spacecraft operations and orbital avoidance against existing automation and ground review. Analyzed how latency, uncertain trajectories, simultaneous maneuvers, and failed coordination affect delegation and redistribute risk among operators.

Used debris capture and SETI to distinguish technical capability from permission to affect another party's interests or confirm a scientific interpretation. Proposed scientific verification through alternative explanations, independent observations, and documented evidence.

Integrated review delays, compliance costs, disclosure risks, and correlated failures into the proposed controls. Developed proportionate reassessment around material changes, reusable evidence, and legally competent institutions, making the burdens of supervision part of the authorization decision.

entries.organization: Small States and the Governance of Strategic Space Dependence
entries.summary: Developed a comparative legal framework for assessing small states' control over foreign-dependent space infrastructure. Analyzed New Zealand's launch regulation, Norway's Arctic satellite partnership, and Luxembourg's LUXEOSys procurement to distinguish permission, ownership, operational rights, and implementation capacity. Proposed an accountable-acceptance standard for strategic dependencies, linking interruption powers and response rights to funded capability. The analysis identifies specific institutional remedies for licensing, service continuity, procurement oversight, and collective action.
entries.detailTitle: Small States and the Governance of Strategic Space Dependence
keyContributions: Built a structured comparison around specific public functions and the decisions needed to perform them. Examined external dependencies, legal and operational rights, domestic capability, and documented outcomes to assess whether retained authority could support an actual public decision.

Identified distinct mechanisms in the three cases: retained launch-permission authority in New Zealand, operational capability through divided responsibilities in Norway, and the planning and legislative information required alongside asset ownership in Luxembourg.

Proposed an accountable-acceptance standard requiring decision makers to identify who can interrupt essential services, which information and rights permit a response, and what funded capacity enables action. Material gaps would require reasoned acceptance or revision before commitment.

Translated the standard into proposed licensing and procurement terms covering operator information, significant changes, suspension, recovery, and service transition. Connected these terms to lifetime costs, technical staffing, and timely legislative scrutiny of financial commitments.

Analyzed collective agency through anti-satellite-testing commitments, UN consensus procedures, and ESA programme and voting rules. Distinguished participation rights, influence, and implementation capacity, connecting national safeguards to collective restraint on debris and cross-border service disruption.

entries.organization: Who May Choose the Lesser Risk: Solar Geoengineering and the Legal Duties of Comparison and Continuity
entries.summary: Developed two proposed legal duties for solar geoengineering: comparative justification and continuity. Connected risk-risk analysis to authorization by requiring proponents to defend policy alternatives and answer challenges from affected constituencies. Traced termination risk to a separation between political control, operator succession, and the physical cooling trajectory. The resulting framework specifies conditions for deployment and withdrawal, supports governed research, and requires continuing assessment of both intervention and nondeployment.
entries.detailTitle: Who May Choose the Lesser Risk: Solar Geoengineering and the Legal Duties of Comparison and Continuity
keyContributions: Separated historical climate conditions, a future without stratospheric aerosol injection, and feasible policy portfolios as distinct comparators. Analyzed how baseline selection, welfare measures, and distributional assumptions shape the case for intervention and the burdens assigned to exposed populations.

Proposed a comparative justification duty requiring proponents to defend alternatives, disclose distributional choices, and answer substantiated objections. Designed powers for independently selected representatives of exposed constituencies to demand redesign or withhold collective approval.

Developed a continuity duty separating programme control, operator choice, and the cooling trajectory. Specified bounded interim succession, independent monitoring, transition finance, and gradual withdrawal so that political authority can change without automatically triggering abrupt physical cessation.

Mapped environmental assessment, notification, and consultation requirements onto the authorization problem. Distinguished limited research from climate-affecting deployment and proposed scrutiny based on expected effects and cumulative scale, including review of related projects together.

Formulated a proposed priority rule for serious threats to subsistence and survival, requiring comparison of feasible alternatives, shared authorization, and credible relief. Built periodic reassessment of forgone benefits and harms of nondeployment into the same decision process.

entries.organization: Mangrove Restoration and the Limits of Compensatory Mitigation: Lessons from Florida for the Greater Bay Area
entries.summary: Developed a comparative legal framework for deciding when ecological restoration can justify new habitat loss. Distinguished protection, repair, and compensatory mitigation across Florida and the Greater Bay Area, using West Lake, Deep Bay, and San Tin to examine evidence of functional replacement. Proposed site-specific baselines, staged authorization and ecological acceptance, funded correction, and continuing responsibility. The framework connects restoration evidence to development permissions, funding decisions, and the point at which obligations can be discharged.
entries.detailTitle: Mangrove Restoration and the Limits of Compensatory Mitigation: Lessons from Florida for the Greater Bay Area
keyContributions: Organized the legal comparison around habitat protection, repair, and compensation for new loss. Traced duties, approval instruments, and administrative powers across Florida, mainland China, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, and Macao to identify how restoration conditions can take legal effect.

Used West Lake to examine hydrological rehabilitation and Deep Bay and San Tin to assess functional replacement. Distinguished canopy growth, construction, and predicted enhancement from evidence supporting compensation, including additionality and the timing of replacement functions.

Proposed staged approval and acceptance separating engineering completion from ecological performance. Specified site baselines, functional objectives, monitoring periods, seasonal coverage, and review authority, linking damaging development phases to the availability of the functions used to justify them.

Designed proposed arrangements for delayed or failed recovery through funded monitoring, correction, and continuing management.
